Q: Forward ValueFromRemainingArguments to function A:

  • A self-declared array - such as [string[]]$Remaining - can not be used to pass named arguments through to another command, e.g. -Target Foo, becomes array @('-Target', 'Foo') and passing $Remaining as-is will pass this array as a single parameter value, i.e. -Target too is part of the parameter value rather than telling PowerShell's parameter binder what parameter to target.

    • Similarly, using splatting with a self-declared array won't work (@Remaining): the array elements are then passed as individual positional arguments, i.e. again as parameter values.

    • Targeting parameters by name requires using a hashtable with splatting, whose entry keys form the target parameter names (sans -, e.g. 'Target') and whose values are the arguments (parameter values; e.g. 'Test')

    • One - cumbersome - option is therefore to do your own parsing of the elements of $Remaining to determine which elements are parameter names vs. values, and construct a hashtable to be used with splatting accordingly. However, with certain limitations there is a much simpler solution - see next point.

  • By contrast, the array stored in the automatic (built-in) $args variable has built-in magic[1] that does allow it to be used for splatting with named arguments.

    • The downside is that $args is only defined in simple, i.e. non-advanced functions and scripts, i.e. those that neither use the [CmdletBindingAttribute()] to decorate their param(...) block nor use a [Parameter()] attribute on any of their parameters.

    • Being only able to use a simple script or function means that you won't get the benefit of automatic support for common parameters such as -ErrorAction or -OutVariable, and the inability to fine-tune parameters with [Parameter()] attributes, such as making parameters mandatory (there's a workaround for that, though - see below). Also, simple scripts/functions do not enforce that only arguments that bind to declared parameters be specified, but that is actually what the solution below relies on - collecting such unbound arguments in array $args.

Simple solution with a non-advanced script, which can therefore utilize $args and its splatting magic:

# Do NOT use a[CmdletBinding()] attribute here.
Param(
  # Do NOT use a [Parameter()] attribute here.
  [ValidateSet('Command1', 'Command2')]
  # Note the use of a `throw` statement as the default value, to emulate
  # a mandatory parameter, though instead of prompting for a value an error is reported.
  $Command = $(throw "Please specify a command")
  # Any additional arguments are implicitly collected by PowerShell
  # in the automatic $args var.
)
function Command1
{
  Param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory)]
    [string]$Target,
    [string]$Option = 'Default'
  )
  "Target: [$Target], Option: [$Option]"
}
# function Command2 # ...

# Here you can use @args to pass *named* arguments through
switch ($Command)
{
  'Command1' { Command1 @args }
  #...
}

Note:

  • The above enforces the -Command parameter as mandatory by throwing an error if no value is bound to it. By contrast, with a [Parameter(Mandatory)] decoration (which isn't an option here, for the reasons discussed), you are prompted for a value by default; to emulate the latter behavior, you can use $Command = (Read-Host "Please specify a command").Trim() - though this simplistic approach won't guard against the user just pressing Enter without having typed a value.
    However, if you use a $(...)-enclosed expression, you're free to place arbitrary code inside, including validation statements.

[1] The magic consists of decorating array elements that represent parameter names with a custom ETS (Extended Type System) property named <CommandParameterName> designating them as such, which splatting then honors. You can verify this with the following command:
& { $args | % { "`n---`n[$_]"; $_ | Get-Member -Type NoteProperty -Force } } -Target Test
Curiously, as the output shows, the parameter name (sans -) is duplicated in the value of the ETS property, and it is in fact only this property value that splatting uses, meaning that the value of the string which the ETS property decorates is technically irrelevant.
Unfortunately, this per-argument decoration approach prevents passing switch parameters with attached values through properly, e.g. -SomeSwitch:$false, though doing so is fortunately not common.

Q: How to change the cursor style for based mode of neovim? A:

To change your cursor in Neovim, see help for guicursor: :h guicursor.

To change your cursor (block by default) to underline (horizontal line) for all modes: set guicursor=a:hor20.

If you prefer a cursor with a vertical line as shape: set guicursor=a:ver20
